stem:
How many signals does ethyl acetate show in its {{1H}} NMR spectrum?
[[mol:CC(=O)OCC|me]]

steps.h: There are three groups with hydrogens: the {{CH3}} on the C=O, the {{OCH2}}, and the {{CH3}} at the end of the ethyl group. Eight hydrogens in all.

ask.q: How many hydrogens does ethyl acetate have?

steps.t: Group the hydrogens that are equivalent
steps.h: The three hydrogens of one {{CH3}} trade places as the group spins, so they are equivalent: one signal per {{CH3}}. The two hydrogens of the {{CH2}} are equivalent to each other.

steps.t: Ask whether any two groups are in the same environment
steps.h: One {{CH3}} is attached to a C=O carbon, the other to a {{CH2}}. Different neighbours, different environments. There is no symmetry that swaps them.

ask.a: No. One is next to C=O, the other next to a {{CH2}}.

steps.h: Three environments: three signals.

solution.rule: One signal for each different environment. Hydrogens swapped by symmetry or by rotation of a {{CH3}} count once.

stem: A {{1H}} NMR spectrum contains a septet (a signal split into seven lines). Which hydrogen gives it?

choices.h: The CH of an isopropyl group: [[mol:CC(C)c1ccccc1|me]]
choices.why: The CH has six equivalent neighbours (two {{CH3}} groups): 6 + 1 = 7.
The {{CH2}} has three neighbours (the {{CH3}}): 3 + 1 = 4 lines, a quartet.

choices.h: The {{CH3}} groups of a tert-butyl group: [[mol:CC(C)(C)c1ccccc1|me]]
choices.why: The carbon next to them has no hydrogens: 0 + 1 = 1 line, a singlet.

choices.h: Any carbon that carries seven hydrogens
choices.why: The number of lines counts the neighbours, plus one. It does not count the hydrogens giving the signal, and no carbon holds seven hydrogens.

steps.h: A hydrogen with n equivalent neighbours on the next carbon appears as n + 1 lines. Seven lines means n = 6.

ask.q: How many neighbouring hydrogens give seven lines?

steps.t: Ask what has six equivalent neighbours
steps.h: Six equivalent hydrogens on neighbouring carbons means two {{CH3}} groups attached to the same carbon.
A CH carrying two {{CH3}} groups is the CH of an isopropyl group, {{(CH3)2CH}}.

ask.q: Which group contains one H with six equivalent neighbours?
ask.a: Isopropyl: the CH between two {{CH3}} groups.

steps.h: The six {{CH3}} hydrogens have one neighbour (the CH), so they appear as a doublet. A septet and a doublet together are the mark of an isopropyl group. On the past exam, a small septet showed that a little isopropylbenzene had formed.

solution.answer: The CH of an isopropyl group, {{(CH3)2CH}}: six equivalent neighbours, 6 + 1 = 7 lines.
solution.rule: n + 1 rule: n equivalent neighbours give n + 1 lines. Septet = isopropyl CH.

stem:
How many signals does methylcyclohexane show in its {{13C}} NMR spectrum?
[[mol:CC1CCCCC1|me]]

steps.h: Seven: the {{CH3}} and six ring carbons. Seven is the most signals there could be.

ask.q: What is the largest possible number of {{13C}} signals here?

steps.h: A mirror plane runs through the {{CH3}}, C1 and C4. It swaps C2 with C6 and C3 with C5.

ask.q: Which ring carbons are swapped by the mirror plane?
ask.a: C2 with C6, and C3 with C5.

steps.h: {{CH3}}; C1; C2 and C6 together; C3 and C5 together; C4.
Five signals. The trap is to answer 7 (no symmetry used) or 4 (forgetting that C1 and C4 are different).

solution.rule: Carbons swapped by a mirror plane or an axis give one signal.

stem: In fluoroethane, which hydrogens are less shielded, and what does that mean? [[mol:CCF|me]]

choices.h: The {{CH2}} hydrogens: fluorine pulls electron density away from them, so they feel more of the external field
choices.why: Less electron density, less shielding, larger net field.

choices.h: The {{CH3}} hydrogens: they are further from fluorine's electrons
choices.why: Shielding comes from the electron density around the hydrogen itself. Fluorine removes that density from the nearer {{CH2}}, not from the {{CH3}}.

choices.h: The {{CH2}} hydrogens: fluorine's lone pairs give them extra electron density
choices.why: Fluorine withdraws electron density through the bonds. Extra density would mean more shielding, not less.

choices.h: Neither: all five hydrogens are in the same environment
choices.why: The {{CH2}} is attached to F and the {{CH3}} is not. Two environments, two signals.

steps.h: The electrons around a nucleus have their own magnetic field, and it counters the external field. The nucleus feels a net field: {{B0}} minus the electrons' field.

ask.q: Does the electrons' field add to the external field or oppose it?
ask.a: It opposes it. That is why it is called shielding.

steps.t: Find where the electrons are pulled away
steps.h: Fluorine is very electronegative. It pulls electron density toward itself, most strongly from the carbon it is attached to and that carbon's hydrogens.

ask.q: Which hydrogens are closer to fluorine?

steps.h: Less electron density around the {{CH2}} hydrogens means less shielding: they feel more of the external field than the {{CH3}} hydrogens do.
Different net fields mean different absorption frequencies. The {{CH2}} and {{CH3}} hydrogens are in different environments and give two separate signals.

solution.answer: The {{CH2}} hydrogens next to F. Fluorine pulls electron density away, so they feel a larger net field.
solution.rule: Net field = B0 minus the electrons' field. Fewer electrons nearby, less shielding.

stem:
How many signals does propane show in its {{1H}} NMR spectrum?
[[mol:CCC|me]]

steps.h: Two {{CH3}} groups and one {{CH2}}.
The molecule is the same from either end, so the two {{CH3}} groups are equivalent: their six hydrogens give one signal.
{{CH3}} hydrogens, one signal. {{CH2}} hydrogens, one signal. Two in all. Answering 3 means counting the groups without checking symmetry, and 8 means counting hydrogens.

solution.rule: Count environments, not hydrogens and not groups.

stem:
How many signals does fluoroethane show in its {{13C}} NMR spectrum?
[[mol:CCF|me]]

steps.h: Two.
C1 carries the fluorine. C2 is a {{CH3}}. They are different.
Two signals. A {{13C}} spectrum counts kinds of carbon. The hydrogens do not enter into it.

solution.rule: 13C NMR: one signal for each different kind of carbon.

stem:
How many signals does acetone show in its {{1H}} NMR spectrum?
[[mol:CC(C)=O|me]]

steps.h: Six, in two {{CH3}} groups. The C=O carbon has none.
The two {{CH3}} groups are both attached to the same C=O and are swapped by a mirror plane: equivalent.
All six hydrogens are in one environment: one signal.

solution.rule: Groups swapped by symmetry share one signal.

stem:
In the {{1H}} NMR spectrum of bromoethane, what does the signal of the {{CH3}} hydrogens look like?
[[mol:CCBr|me]]

choices.why: Two neighbouring hydrogens on the {{CH2}}: 2 + 1 = 3.
That uses the {{CH3}}'s own three hydrogens: 3 + 1. The rule counts the neighbours. The quartet is the {{CH2}} signal.
A singlet needs zero neighbouring hydrogens. The next carbon has two.
That takes n as the number of lines. The rule is n + 1.

steps.h: The carbon next to the {{CH3}} is the {{CH2}}, which has 2 hydrogens.
n = 2, so 2 + 1 = 3 lines: a triplet.

steps.t: Do not count the hydrogens themselves
steps.h: The three {{CH3}} hydrogens are equivalent to each other and do not split their own signal. (The {{CH2}} signal, with 3 neighbours, is a quartet.)

solution.rule: Lines = neighbours + 1, counting the hydrogens on the next carbon.

stem: What does it mean to say that electrons shield a nucleus in NMR?

choices.h: The electrons' magnetic field counters the external field, so the nucleus feels a smaller net field
choices.why: This is the lecture's definition: {{B0}} minus the electrons' field.

choices.h: The electrons add their field to the external field, so the nucleus feels a larger net field
choices.why: The electrons' field opposes the external one. A larger net field is what a less shielded nucleus feels.

choices.h: The electrons absorb the light before it reaches the nucleus
choices.why: Shielding is about magnetic fields, not about blocking light.

choices.h: The electrons stop the nucleus from aligning with the field at all
choices.why: The nuclei still align with or against the field. Shielding only changes the size of the field they feel.

steps.h: The sample sits in an external magnetic field, {{B0}}.
Electrons have their own magnetic field, and it counters the external field.
The nucleus feels a net field of {{B0}} minus the electrons' field. Nuclei with different amounts of electron density around them feel different net fields and give different signals.

solution.answer: The electrons' own magnetic field counters the external field, so the nucleus feels a smaller net field.
solution.rule: Net magnetic field = B0 minus the electrons' field.

stem:
How many signals does bromoethene show in its {{1H}} NMR spectrum?
[[mol:C=CBr]]

steps.h: Three: one on the carbon that carries Br, two on the {{CH2}} end.

steps.t: Remember that a double bond does not rotate
steps.h: The two hydrogens of the {{CH2}} end are locked in place. One is on the same side of the double bond as Br (cis to it), the other is on the opposite side (trans).
Three different environments: three signals. The trap is to treat the two {{CH2}} hydrogens as equivalent, as they would be on a carbon that can rotate.

solution.rule: Across a C=C there is no rotation: the two H of a =CH2 are different unless the other end carries two identical groups.

stem:
How many signals does cyclohexane show in its {{1H}} NMR spectrum at room temperature?
[[mol:C1CCCCC1]]

steps.h: A chair has six axial and six equatorial hydrogens, which looks like two environments.
The ring flips rapidly at room temperature (K = 1), and every axial hydrogen becomes equatorial and the reverse. Each hydrogen spends half its time in each position.
On average all twelve hydrogens are the same: one signal. All six carbons are also equivalent.

solution.rule: Hydrogens that trade places quickly (ring flip, rotation of a {{CH3}}) give one averaged signal.

stem:
How many signals does ethyl acetate show in its {{13C}} NMR spectrum?
[[mol:CC(=O)OCC|me]]

steps.h: Four: the {{CH3}} on the C=O, the C=O carbon, the {{OCH2}}, and the end {{CH3}}.
There is none. Every carbon has different neighbours.
Four signals. The C=O carbon has no hydrogens but still gives a {{13C}} signal: answering 3 means it was left out.

solution.rule: 13C NMR counts every kind of carbon, including carbons with no hydrogens.

stem: A compound shows two {{1H}} NMR signals: a septet for 1 H and a doublet for 6 H. Which compound is it?

choices.why: The CH has six neighbours (septet) and the six {{CH3}} hydrogens have one neighbour (doublet).
1-Chloropropane has three environments, so three signals, and none of its hydrogens has six neighbours.
All nine hydrogens are equivalent and have no neighbours: one singlet.
Chloroethane gives a triplet (3 H) and a quartet (2 H): the pattern of an ethyl group.

steps.h: Seven lines: a hydrogen with six equivalent neighbours.
Two lines: hydrogens with one neighbour. Six of them means two equivalent {{CH3}} groups next to one CH.
{{(CH3)2CH}}, an isopropyl group, and nothing else with hydrogens: 2-chloropropane.

solution.rule: Septet (1 H) plus doublet (6 H) = isopropyl.

stem:
Into how many lines is the {{CH2}} signal of diethyl ether split?
[[mol:CCOCC|me]]

steps.h: On one side is its {{CH3}}, with 3 hydrogens. On the other side is the oxygen, which has no hydrogens.

steps.t: Do not count across the oxygen
steps.h: The other {{CH2}} is not on a neighbouring carbon, and it is equivalent to this one anyway. Only the 3 hydrogens of the {{CH3}} count.
3 + 1 = 4 lines, a quartet. Answering 6 comes from counting the two {{CH3}} groups together, and 3 from forgetting the + 1.

solution.rule: Count only the hydrogens on the carbons directly attached to the carbon in question.

stem:
What does the {{1H}} NMR spectrum of 1,2-dichloroethane look like?
[[mol:ClCCCl]]

choices.why: All four hydrogens are equivalent, and equivalent hydrogens do not split each other.
The two hydrogens on the next carbon are equivalent to the ones being observed, so they cause no splitting.
The two {{CH2}} groups are swapped by the molecule's symmetry. They are one environment, not two.

choices.h: Four signals, one for each hydrogen
choices.why: Signals count environments, not hydrogens.

steps.h: The molecule is the same from both ends, so the two {{CH2}} groups are equivalent. All four hydrogens are in one environment: one signal.
The n + 1 rule counts neighbours that are different from the hydrogens giving the signal. Equivalent hydrogens do not split each other.
One signal with no splitting: a singlet. The trap is to see two hydrogens on the next carbon and call it a triplet.

solution.rule: Equivalent hydrogens do not split each other.

stem:
How many signals does 1,4-dimethylbenzene show in its {{13C}} NMR spectrum?
[[mol:Cc1ccc(C)cc1|me]]

steps.h: Eight: two {{CH3}} and six ring carbons.

The two ends of the molecule are the same, and so are the two sides. The two {{CH3}} carbons are equivalent. The two ring carbons that carry a {{CH3}} are equivalent. The four ring CH carbons are all equivalent.
Three kinds of carbon: three signals. Answering 4 usually means splitting the four ring CH carbons into two sets, and 2 means forgetting that ring carbons with and without a {{CH3}} differ.

solution.rule: High symmetry means few signals: find every mirror plane before counting.

stem: Which compound shows exactly two {{1H}} NMR signals, both singlets?

choices.why: Two different {{CH3}} groups, each next to an atom with no hydrogens.
Acetone's two {{CH3}} groups are equivalent: one singlet, not two.
Two signals, but the {{CH3}} is a triplet and the {{CH2}} is a quartet.
Ethyl acetate has three signals: a singlet, a quartet and a triplet.

steps.h: Two signals means two environments. Both singlets means neither kind of hydrogen has a different hydrogen on the next carbon.
One {{CH3}} is on the C=O carbon and one is on the oxygen. They are different, and each is attached to an atom with no hydrogens: two singlets.
Acetone has one signal. Diethyl ether has two signals, but they are a triplet and a quartet. Ethyl acetate has three signals.

solution.rule: A singlet means no hydrogens on the neighbouring atoms (or only equivalent ones).

stem:
How many signals does the allyl cation show in its {{13C}} NMR spectrum?
[[mol:C=C[CH2+]]]

steps.h: The positive charge and the double bond trade ends: {{CH2=CH-CH2+}} and {{+CH2-CH=CH2}} are two pictures of one ion.

steps.t: See what resonance does to the ends
steps.h: The real ion is the average of the two pictures, so the two end carbons are identical: each carries half of the positive charge.
Two kinds of carbon, the two ends and the middle: two signals. Answering 3 comes from reading one resonance structure as the real molecule.

solution.rule: Atoms made equivalent by resonance give one signal.
